title: Farther the Shift, Sparser the Representation: Analyzing OOD Mechanisms in LLMs
claim: Across several independent difficulty axes, a measured internal property shifts monotonically as inputs get harder, revealing a consistent systematic trend.
layout: 4 panels in a row, each with an Easy-to-Hard arrow beneath
description: A single wide strip of four small statistical plots, each titled with a paper section number: Reasoning Complexity, Answer Choice, Knowledge Conflict and Context Length. Panel 1 is a bar chart over difficulty levels 1 to 5, with bars darkening from light to dark blue. Panel 2 is a bar chart with three bars (Normal, Moderate, Large). Panel 3 is a box plot comparing Non-Conflict and Conflict. Panel 4 is a box plot over context lengths from original to 128k. The y-axis is the sparsity score (Top10 Energy), and the left axis is labeled Dense to Sparse. Every panel shows the value rising with difficulty. A blue palette runs from light to dark with increasing difficulty. Under each panel an Easy to Hard arrow reinforces the shared trend. The eye goes first to the rising bars on the left and the clear upward staircase in the rightmost panel.
caption: Harder Inputs Induce Sparser Representations. Across all four controlled difficulty axes, the last hidden states become progressively sparser as tasks get harder. Results are shown for \exampleb{Qwen2.5-3B} using Top-10% Energy; nevertheless, the same trend holds across difficulty datasets and settings, sparsity metrics, LLM family, and LLM sizes.
abstract: In this work, we investigate how the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) change with inputs of increasing difficulty. Although sparsity changes may not be obvious for individual samples, dataset-level results reveal a consistent statistical trend: as task difficulty increases (e.g., harder questions, longer contexts, or more answer choices), the last hidden states of LLMs become systematically sparser. In short, \textbf{the harder the task, the sparser the representation}. This sparsity--difficulty relation is observable across diverse models and domains, suggesting that harder inputs drive more concentrated activation patterns in the last hidden state. Through a series of controlled analyses and learning-dynamics experiments, we show that representational density is a learned property of data familiarity: models develop rich, distributed representations for mastered patterns, while unfamiliar inputs default to sparser activations. Our finding is also actionable. We illustrate this with Sparsity-Guided Curriculum In-Context Learning (SG-ICL), which uses sparsity to select few-shot demonstrations matched to the query's difficulty, outperforming standard CoT and Auto-CoT baselines on MATH-500. Our study provides new insights into how LLM representations reflect task difficulty and how this signal can be leveraged for inference. The source code is available at the URL: https://github.com/MingyuJ666/sparsityLLM.
